title: Partial stream cancel -> memory accumulation oncall notes
content:
Summary:
During a one-week window we observed a steady host heap increase on a subset of streaming frontends serving hosted-api. The growth correlated with higher rates of client-side stream cancellations (client closed websocket / HTTP2 stream mid-response). Impact was elevated memory pressure, increased eviction activity, and several hosts hitting transient OOM safeguards causing pod restarts and degraded tail latency for tenant production traffic.

Why this is odd:
- We already have cancellation propagation in our request handler.
- Growth only occurs when responses are large (>8k tokens) and client cancels before completion.
- Reproducible locally under a synthetic client that cancels after receiving N chunks.

Timeline (high level):
- 2025-11-06 02:10 UTC: First alert from host-heap-90pct on worker pool alpha-3.
- 2025-11-06 02:18 UTC: SRE oncall begins triage; notices concurrent elevated streaming cancel rate in streaming-metrics dashboard.
- 2025-11-06 02:35 UTC: Temporary mitigation: lowered max-stream-concurrency on alpha pool and enabled token-shedder for bursty tenants. Memory rise stabilizes but not eliminated.
- 2025-11-06 04:10 UTC: Repro script (stress-canceler) reproduces host heap growth locally within 10 minutes.
- 2025-11-07 09:00 UTC: Root-cause hypothesis refined after heap profiles and pprof traces.

Technical findings:
- Heap profiles show many large buffer objects (response-chunk buffers, per-request prefix cache refs) retained with goroutines in a 'waiting' state. Stack traces point to streaming write loop waiting on outbound queue that is never drained after client cancel path.
- Cancellation was observed to close the transport but in some code paths the per-request outbound queue owner kept a reference to the buffer slice (buffer pool lease not returned).
- Interaction with continuous-batching: when an in-flight microbatch contains canceled requests, the batch completion callback assumed batch members would always call `releaseBuffers()`; canceled items take an alternate code path that did not trigger release in one edge case.
- A secondary factor: aggressive prefix/KV cache retention held references to tokenized prefixes for canceled requests because eviction heuristics consider request as still active until batch lifecycle completes.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- Patch: added a defensive finalizer in the streaming mux to force-release outbound buffers on transport closure (hotfix rolled to canary 2025-11-06 06:00 UTC).
- Config: reduced continuous-batching window on affected pools to shorten the time canceled requests could linger in batches.
- Alerting: created streaming-cancel-rate anomaly alert (sensitivity: 5x baseline) and host-buffer-leak-rate metric (counts leaked buffer returns).

Long-term fixes and action items:
- Code fix (PR referenced above): ensure every cancel code path routes through a single release path for buffers and batch membership; add unit/integration tests that simulate mid-batch cancellations. Owner: eng-serving-runtime (Ravi). ETA: 2025-11-20.
- Batching lifecycle: add explicit state transitions and invariants to microbatch manager so items marked canceled cannot hold cache-refs beyond batch finalize. Owner: eng-serving-runtime (Diego). ETA: 2025-12-05.
- Metrics and invariants: instrument buffer pool to emit (alloc, return, outstanding) with tenant tags. Add an invariant alarm when outstanding increases > 0.5% over a 15m window. Owner: eng-observability (Lina). ETA: 2025-11-17.
- E2E repro harness: fold stress-canceler into CI to prevent regressions. Owner: eng-dx. ETA: 2025-11-13.

Runbook additions (short):
- If host-heap trend > 20% / 30m and streaming-cancel-rate > 3x baseline: 1) disable microbatching on affected pool, 2) enable token-shedder fallback, 3) schedule a canary deploy of the hotfix.
- Quick triage commands: `kubectl top nodes --selector=pool=alpha` ; `curl $OBS/streaming-cancel-rate?pool=alpha` ; `pprof heap http://$POD:6060/debug/pprof/heap > /tmp/heap.pb`

Open questions and risks:
- Are there other codepaths (e.g., function-calling tool outputs, embeddings streaming shim) that share the same release assumption?
- Hotfix uses a defensive finalizer; it's safe but not ideal long-term—must ensure no double-free semantics.
- Operational risk: lowering batching window increases token cost; need to weigh cost vs stability until permanent fix deployed.

Notes to the oncall successor:
- Watch the new buffer pool metrics for regressions. If buffer outstanding count persists after hotfix deploy, escalate to eng-serving-runtime and attach pprof from a failing host.
- Correlate with client-side logs if possible; if a tenant has many mid-stream cancels they may be misusing streaming API semantics.

Appendix (repro steps):
1) Start local serving-runtime with small batch window (10ms) and attach the stress-canceler script.
2) stress-canceler opens N=100 concurrent streams, requests 12k-token responses, cancels after receiving 3 chunks.
3) Observe `go tool pprof` snapshots every 2 minutes; confirm leaked buffers in stacks `streamMux.writeLoop` and `microbatch.finalize`.

Updated: 2025-11-10 - added runbook entries and owners after post-incident sync.
